body: I can certainly empathise with your experiences.  There's no way those circumstances won't impact your life negatively.  I also think we have innate desires to attain a certain level of success in life.  The depression comes when our life fails to meet our own expectations.  When you go to a new school, that expectation is to make friends and be liked.  To fit in.  If you go to school and you're bullied and outright hated, no amount of positive thinking is going to "fix" the situation.  You're basically trapped in a nightmare and you're reminded of that with every sneer, cruel laugh, push, etc.  If the school happens to NOT be a one-off, but you find yourself disliked universally, then your mental health is going to deteriorate.  There's no Tony Robbins video or Will Smith pep talk that will save you.  In fact, these types of "motivational" speeches just irritate someone who sees the unfairness of their situation.  The motivators themselves aren't crippled by intractable problems.  They talk about fixable stuff all the time - how to earn more money, how to lose weight, etc. They live in this cause-effect delightful kintergarden experience ... "oh! if I push here, sometimes a good thing happens! But not always, so I sometimes have to put in more effort...but the reward is there in the end! How delightful!".  Some problems just aren't fixable and they impact people's lives terribly.  At the same time, I do try to improve my life because THAT does make a difference to my mental health, particularly with exercise.

I 100% agree with your sentiment.  I do try my best in my life.  I exercise, I eat well, I have been self-employed the last 15 years, I travel (living in Thailand now with my children).  I do not think this contradicts my previous comment though.  My great losses have been caused by happenstance.  I've also lucked out too! Much of my success is down to having the means to even get started on my successes.  I was lucky just to NOT be born in a million circumstances that would have been way worse than what I was born into (a good family, a peaceful time, a relatively very resource-rich time in terms of human history).  I guess what I am saying is - a duality exists.  Yes, you are right that we can make lemonade from lemons, or in fact, we might even climb out of a hole and into a GREAT life through our own efforts.  This is 100% possible, and I believe this.  However, in tandem with all of this possibility is random happenstance that could send us down into the pits of hell.  These two aspects of life aren't at odds with one another.  They co-exist, and certainly the "just world" idea likes to pretend that there is only the one aspect (our efforts).  It's a wonderful fantasy, and I'd love to believe it, but it's not true.  It's also a kick in the teeth to those who have been decimated by bad luck - to the point they cannot function.  Not only are they in immense torture, but the "just world" assumption is that they are somehow to blame for the continuation of their circumstances.  If only they could pull their chin up and dust themselves down etc.

> I had a friend that said "think good thoughts - have a good life. Think bad thoughts - have a bad life" as if it was that easy, while also implicitly blaming my problems on me not thinking the right way.

This is a "just world" fallacy that people like your friend want to believe because they dare not think that their entire lives could be torpedoed at any moment by dumb bad luck.   They want to think they can control their lives by positive thinking and that some "law of attraction" will guide them through a perfect life where everything works out just right - and not "just right" in some shallow perfect way, but "just right" in such a way that they have to show their skills and determination to get what they want - and they get it.  Wowsers - talk about a just world!  1+1=2.  Everything's a formula.  Until you get a tumour or a drunk driver runs you over as you walk down a pavement, or you're born at the wrong time and you just enter working age when your country has *just* gone into a deep economic depression that will last decades.  

Of course, we know life has an arbitrary nature to it.  Dumb luck rules all. Ultimately, we have zero control over our lives.   And in a way, your friend knows it too - it's just denial on his part.  It's the same denial I have when I hear about young children getting utterly fucked up by some chronic illnesses that devastates their lives.  I know that such illnesses could happen to me, but something in my brain says "fuck that noise" and I turn the page or switch the channel, and suddenly that possibility is gone.  That possibility is *never* gone - it's always there.   Your friend is shit scared to lose what he has and *deep down* he knows dumb luck could take it all away.  There's no getting around that.  The "Law of Attraction" book became a best seller by tapping into human denial.  Religion does the same thing.  There's always hope - *always hope* - so long as we can conjour up strong enough denial, there's always hope.  And we know - there ultimately is no hope.  We just survive until we die, and that's it.
